claim: More than 20 recurrent missense gain-of-function (GOF) mutations have been identified in the sodium-activated potassium (KNa) channel gene KCNT1 in patients with severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs).
source: More than 20 recurrent missense gain-of-function (GOF) mutations have been identified in the sodium-activated potassium (KNa) channel gene KCNT1 in patients with severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs), most of which are resistant to current therapies.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field of KCNT1-related epilepsies and is presented as a factual statement in the abstract.

claim: Most KCNT1-related DEEs are resistant to current therapies.
source: More than 20 recurrent missense gain-of-function (GOF) mutations have been identified in the sodium-activated potassium (KNa) channel gene KCNT1 in patients with severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs), most of which are resistant to current therapies.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about KCNT1-related epilepsies and their treatment resistance.

claim: The Kcnt1Y777H variant had no effects on glutamatergic or VIP neuron function.
source: Although the Kcnt1Y777H variant had no effects on glutamatergic or VIP neuron function, it increased subthreshold KNa currents in both SST and PV neurons but with opposite effects on neuronal output
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from current-clamp recordings and voltage-clamp experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Kcnt1Y777H variant increased subthreshold KNa currents in both SST and PV neurons.
source: Although the Kcnt1Y777H variant had no effects on glutamatergic or VIP neuron function, it increased subthreshold KNa currents in both SST and PV neurons but with opposite effects on neuronal output
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp experimental data measuring KNa currents in SST and PV neurons.

claim: SST neurons became hypoexcitable with a higher rheobase current and lower action potential (AP) firing frequency due to the Kcnt1Y777H variant.
source: SST neurons became hypoexcitable with a higher rheobase current and lower action potential (AP) firing frequency, whereas PV neurons became hyperexcitable with a lower rheobase current and higher AP firing frequency.
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp experimental data showing altered membrane properties and AP firing in SST neurons.

claim: PV neurons became hyperexcitable with a lower rheobase current and higher AP firing frequency due to the Kcnt1Y777H variant.
source: SST neurons became hypoexcitable with a higher rheobase current and lower action potential (AP) firing frequency, whereas PV neurons became hyperexcitable with a lower rheobase current and higher AP firing frequency.
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp experimental data showing altered membrane properties and AP firing in PV neurons.

claim: The differential effects of the Kcnt1Y777H variant on SST and PV neurons are not likely due to inherent differences in these neuron types.
source: Further neurophysiological and computational modeling experiments showed that the differential effects of the Kcnt1Y777H variant on SST and PV neurons are not likely due to inherent differences in these neuron types, but to an increased persistent sodium current in PV, but not SST, neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling experiments and experimental data comparing SST and PV neurons.

claim: An increased persistent sodium current in PV, but not SST, neurons accounts for the differential effects of the Kcnt1Y777H variant.
source: Further neurophysiological and computational modeling experiments showed that the differential effects of the Kcnt1Y777H variant on SST and PV neurons are not likely due to inherent differences in these neuron types, but to an increased persistent sodium current in PV, but not SST, neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of persistent sodium current and computational modeling showing this current is sufficient to explain the hyperexcitability in PV neurons.

claim: The Kcnt1Y777H variant increased excitatory input onto SST neurons.
source: The Kcnt1Y777H variant also increased excitatory input onto, and chemical and electrical synaptic connectivity between, SST neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data measuring spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) onto SST neurons.

claim: The Kcnt1Y777H variant increased chemical and electrical synaptic connectivity between SST neurons.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature documenting KCNT1 variants in patients.

claim: KCNT1 is activated by a persistent inward sodium leak (NaP) current at rest in some neuronal types.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on KCNT1 activation mechanisms.

source: Thus, although heterozygous Kcnt1Y777H expression resulted in similar KNa current increases and neuronal physiology effects to those found with homozygous Kcnt1Y777H expression, the broad effects on synaptic connectivity and activity found in YH-HOM networks were absent in YH-HET networks, which likely results in the observed reduction in seizure incidence in heterozygous, relative to homozygous, mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of heterozygous and homozygous experimental data.

claim: The absence of broad network effects in YH-HET networks likely results in the observed reduction in seizure incidence in heterozygous, relative to homozygous, mice.
source: Thus, although heterozygous Kcnt1Y777H expression resulted in similar KNa current increases and neuronal physiology effects to those found with homozygous Kcnt1Y777H expression, the broad effects on synaptic connectivity and activity found in YH-HOM networks were absent in YH-HET networks, which likely results in the observed reduction in seizure incidence in heterozygous, relative to homozygous, mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of network effects and seizure phenotypes.

claim: About 80–90% of cortical GABAergic neurons fall into three, largely non-overlapping populations that can be identified by their expression of unique markers: PV (~40%), SST (~30%), and VIP (~15%).
source: About 80–90% of cortical GABAergic neurons fall into three, largely non-overlapping populations that can be identified by their expression of unique markers: the Ca2+-binding protein PV (~40%), the neuropeptides SST (~30%), and VIP (~15%) (Rudy et al., 2011; Tremblay et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature characterizing GABAergic neuron populations.

claim: The majority of PV-expressing neurons have been characterized as FS.
source: The majority of PV-expressing neurons have been characterized as FS, and VIP-expressing as NFS, whereas SST-expressing neurons, although largely thought to show NFS firing properties, also contain a population that exhibits an FS-like phenotype (Large et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature characterizing GABAergic neuron firing properties.

claim: VIP-expressing neurons have been characterized as NFS.
source: The majority of PV-expressing neurons have been characterized as FS, and VIP-expressing as NFS, whereas SST-expressing neurons, although largely thought to show NFS firing properties, also contain a population that exhibits an FS-like phenotype (Large et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature characterizing GABAergic neuron firing properties.

claim: SST-expressing neurons, although largely thought to show NFS firing properties, also contain a population that exhibits an FS-like phenotype.
source: The majority of PV-expressing neurons have been characterized as FS, and VIP-expressing as NFS, whereas SST-expressing neurons, although largely thought to show NFS firing properties, also contain a population that exhibits an FS-like phenotype (Large et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature characterizing GABAergic neuron firing properties.

claim: KCNT1 is expressed at higher levels in both human and mouse cortical GABAergic neurons expressing PV and SST, than in those expressing VIP.
source: KCNT1 is expressed at higher levels in both human and mouse cortical GABAergic neurons expressing PV and SST, than in those expressing VIP (Gertler et al., 2022; Shore et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on KCNT1 expression patterns.

claim: Current-clamp recordings from YH-HET VIP neurons revealed no significant effect of the variant on any of the membrane or AP properties measured.
source: Current-clamp recordings from YH-HET VIP neurons revealed no significant effect of the variant on any of the membrane or AP properties measured (Figure 4B1).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp experimental data shown in Figure 4B1.

claim: YH-HET SST neurons showed a strong decrease in input resistance, with an accompanying increase in rheobase current, relative to those of WT SST neurons.
source: Conversely, YH-HET SST neurons showed a strong decrease in input resistance, with an accompanying increase in rheobase current, relative to those of WT SST neurons (Figure 4B2), similar to the hypoexcitable membrane phenotype observed in the YH-HET NFS neurons, without altering AP shape parameters.
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp experimental data shown in Figure 4B2.

claim: YH-HET SST neurons showed a reduction in the membrane time constant and an increase in membrane capacitance.
source: YH-HET SST neurons also showed a reduction in the membrane time constant and an increase in membrane capacitance, which was accompanied by an increase in soma size (Supplementary file 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), compared with those of WT SST neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp experimental data shown in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: YH-HET SST neurons showed an increase in soma size compared with those of WT SST neurons.
source: YH-HET SST neurons also showed a reduction in the membrane time constant and an increase in membrane capacitance, which was accompanied by an increase in soma size (Supplementary file 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), compared with those of WT SST neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: YH-HET PV neurons exhibited a decrease in the rheobase current compared with that of WT.
source: Unexpectedly, YH-HET PV neurons exhibited a decrease in the rheobase current compared with that of WT (Figure 4B3), and an increase in AP amplitude (Supplementary file 2), suggesting the Kcnt1Y777H variant increases PV neuron excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp experimental data shown in Figure 4B3.

claim: YH-HET PV neurons showed an increase in AP amplitude.
source: Unexpectedly, YH-HET PV neurons exhibited a decrease in the rheobase current compared with that of WT (Figure 4B3), and an increase in AP amplitude (Supplementary file 2), suggesting the Kcnt1Y777H variant increases PV neuron excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp experimental data shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The AP firing frequencies across increasing current steps were indistinguishable between WT and YH-HET VIP neurons.
source: Consistent with a lack of any effects on membrane and AP shape properties, the AP firing frequencies across increasing current steps were indistinguishable between WT and YH-HET VIP neurons (Figure 4C1).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp experimental data shown in Figure 4C1.

claim: YH-HET SST neurons fired fewer APs across all current steps relative to WT SST neurons.
source: As expected, based on their hypoexcitable membrane properties, the YH-HET SST neurons fired fewer APs across all current steps relative to WT SST neurons (Figure 4C2).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp experimental data shown in Figure 4C2.

claim: YH-HET PV neurons fired more APs across all current steps relative to their WT counterparts.
source: In contrast to SST neurons, but consistent with their decreased rheobase current, YH-HET PV neurons fired more APs across all current steps relative to their WT counterparts (Figure 4C3).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp experimental data shown in Figure 4C3.

claim: Both WT and YH-HET PV neurons responded similarly to increased temperature.
source: Notably, although these experiments were performed at room temperature (~22°C), and increasing temperatures to 35°C altered multiple neuronal physiology parameters (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), both WT and YH-HET PV neurons responded similarly to increased temperature (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B), suggesting that the observed phenotypes are not temperature dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp experimental data at different temperatures shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The observed phenotypes in PV neurons are not temperature dependent.
source: Notably, although these experiments were performed at room temperature (~22°C), and increasing temperatures to 35°C altered multiple neuronal physiology parameters (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), both WT and YH-HET PV neurons responded similarly to increased temperature (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B), suggesting that the observed phenotypes are not temperature dependent.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing similar temperature responses between WT and YH-HET PV neurons.

claim: The same ion channel mutation can lead to opposite effects on excitability in the two largest GABAergic neuron subtypes.
source: Together, these data showed that, as hypothesized, KCNT1 GOF indeed strongly reduces the excitability of SST neurons, but unexpectedly, it also causes a hyperexcitable effect in PV neurons; thus, the same ion channel mutation can lead to opposite effects on excitability in the two largest GABAergic neuron subtypes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing opposite effects in SST and PV neurons.

claim: YH-HET VIP neuron KNa currents were not different from those of WT at any voltage step.
source: For YH-HET VIP neurons, pairwise comparisons to assess voltage-dependent differences showed that their KNa currents were not different from those of WT at any voltage step (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B1, C1).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B1 and C1.

claim: YH-HET SST neurons showed significant increases in KNa currents compared with those of WT across multiple subthreshold voltage steps, including −60, −50, and −40 mV.
source: On the other hand, YH-HET SST neurons showed significant increases in KNa currents compared with those of WT across multiple subthreshold voltage steps, including −60, −50, and −40 mV (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B2, C2)
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B2 and C2.

claim: KNa currents were not different between YH-HET and WT PV neurons at any voltage step using TTX subtraction.
source: Somewhat unexpectedly, pairwise comparisons showed that KNa currents were not different between YH-HET and WT PV neurons at any voltage step (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B3, C3).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp experimental data using TTX subtraction shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B3 and C3.

claim: VU0606170 (VU170) is a small-molecule, selective KCNT1 channel inhibitor.
source: However, more recently, we identified and validated a small-molecule, selective KCNT1 channel inhibitor termed VU0606170 or VU170 (Spitznagel et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work identifying and validating VU170.

claim: There is a non-specific outward VU-sensitive current in Kcnt1−/−; Kcnt2−/− double knockout neurons that started around −10 mV and peaked at +50 mV.
source: This analysis indicated a non-specific outward VU-sensitive current that started around −10 mV and peaked at +50 mV (~1 nA peak current compared with ~3 nA in WT neurons), which was not present using TTX subtraction (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp experimental data in knockout neurons shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Across negative potentials, there was an inward TTX-sensitive current in Kcnt1−/−; Kcnt2−/− double knockout neurons, which is likely due to the persistent Na+ current.
source: Across negative potentials, there was an inward TTX-sensitive current, which again is likely due to the persistent Na+ current, whereas there was little to no outward VU-sensitive current (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), validating the utility of VU170 in isolating KNa currents across this voltage range.
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp experimental data in knockout neurons shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and inference about the persistent Na+ current.

claim: VU170 is validated for isolating KNa currents across negative voltage ranges.
source: Across negative potentials, there was an inward TTX-sensitive current, which again is likely due to the persistent Na+ current, whereas there was little to no outward VU-sensitive current (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), validating the utility of VU170 in isolating KNa currents across this voltage range.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental validation data in knockout neurons.

claim: In all three WT GABAergic neuron subtypes, subtraction of the VU170 trace from the control trace revealed nA-sized outward currents at depolarized potentials.
source: In all three WT GABAergic neuron subtypes, subtraction of the VU170 trace from the control trace revealed nA-sized outward currents at depolarized potentials, and in YH-HET neurons, the overall VU170-sensitive current was increased relative to those of WT, as measured by a significant effect of genotype using a linear model (Figure 5A1–3, B1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp experimental data using VU170 shown in Figure 5A1-3 and B1-3.

claim: In YH-HET neurons, the overall VU170-sensitive current was increased relative to those of WT.
source: In all three WT GABAergic neuron subtypes, subtraction of the VU170 trace from the control trace revealed nA-sized outward currents at depolarized potentials, and in YH-HET neurons, the overall VU170-sensitive current was increased relative to those of WT, as measured by a significant effect of genotype using a linear model (Figure 5A1–3, B1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp experimental data using VU170 and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A1-3 and B1-3.

claim: For YH-HET VIP neurons, a significant increase in the VU170 current was only observed at +50 mV.
source: For YH-HET VIP neurons, a significant increase in the VU170 current was only observed at +50 mV (Figure 5B1), whereas subthreshold currents were indistinguishable from those of WT (Figure 5C1).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp experimental data using VU170 and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B1 and C1.

claim: In YH-HET SST neurons, significant increases in VU170-sensitive current occurred at more negative voltage steps, from −60 to −30 mV.
source: Conversely, in YH-HET SST neurons, significant increases occurred at more negative voltage steps, from −60 to −30 mV (Figure 5C2).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp experimental data using VU170 and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C2.

claim: YH-HET PV neurons showed an increase in VU170-sensitive currents, with significant increases from −70 to −50 mV.
source: In contrast to the TTX results, YH-HET PV neurons showed an increase in VU170-sensitive currents, with significant increases from −70 to −50 mV (Figure 5C3).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp experimental data using VU170 and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C3.

claim: PV neurons showed subthreshold-specific KNa current increases that were highly similar to, and overlapping with, those of SST neurons.
source: On the other hand, PV neurons showed subthreshold-specific KNa current increases that were highly similar to, and overlapping with, those of SST neurons; thus, differential KNa current increases alone likely do not account for the opposite effects of KCNT1 GOF on physiology observed in these two neuron types.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of voltage-clamp experimental data in SST and PV neurons.

claim: Differential KNa current increases alone likely do not account for the opposite effects of KCNT1 GOF on physiology observed in SST and PV neurons.
source: On the other hand, PV neurons showed subthreshold-specific KNa current increases that were highly similar to, and overlapping with, those of SST neurons; thus, differential KNa current increases alone likely do not account for the opposite effects of KCNT1 GOF on physiology observed in these two neuron types.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of KNa current data and excitability phenotypes.

claim: Introducing KCNT1 GOF at the lower level (EC50 = 35 mM) into model VIP neurons did not alter their AP firing rate, input resistance, or rheobase.
source: Consistent with our experimental data, introducing KCNT1 GOF at the lower level (EC50 = 35 mM) into model VIP neurons did not alter their AP firing rate, input resistance, or rheobase
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data.

claim: At the higher level of KCNT1 GOF (EC50 = 30 mM), model VIP neurons showed small changes in input resistance and rheobase, but these changes were not sufficient to affect the AP firing rate.
source: whereas at the higher level (EC50 = 30 mM), there were small changes in input resistance (40 mM: 266.5 ± 28.2; 30 mM: 264.8 ± 28.0, p = 0.012) and rheobase (40 mM: 78.7 ± 11.6; 30 mM: 80.4 ± 11.1, p = 0.014), but these changes were not sufficient to affect the AP firing rate (Figure 6E1, E2, Supplementary file 3, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 6E1, E2, Supplementary file 3, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Model SST neurons with KCNT1 GOF at both levels fired fewer APs per current step as the GOF was increased, and showed significantly reduced input resistances, higher rheobases, and lower AP firing rates.
source: On the other hand, model SST neurons with KCNT1 GOF at both levels fired fewer APs per current step as the GOF was increased, and showed significantly reduced input resistances, higher rheobases, and lower AP firing rates (Figure 6F1, F2 and Supplementary file 3), results that agree with our experimental observations.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 6F1, F2 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Model PV neurons responded to KCNT1 GOF with decreased input resistance, increased rheobase, and a reduced AP firing rate, in contrast to experimental data.
source: In contrast to experimental data, but similar to model SST neurons, model PV neurons responded to KCNT1 GOF with decreased input resistance, increased rheobase, and a reduced AP firing rate (Figure 6G1, G2 and Supplementary file 3), although the magnitude of these effects were smaller than those in model SST neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 6G1, G2 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The increased excitability observed in YH-HET PV neurons is not simply due to an intrinsic property of this GABAergic subtype.
source: These data suggest that the increased excitability observed in YH-HET PV neurons is not simply due to an intrinsic property of this GABAergic subtype, but instead results from an indirect mechanism (e.g. a compensatory response like an increase in Na+ channels) or depends on a feature of KCNT1 function not captured by the model.
evidence: This claim is inferred from discrepancy between modeling and experimental data.

claim: Inserting KCNT1 channels with SST kinetics into VIP and glutamatergic neurons enhanced the GOF effects on input resistance and rheobase, and resulted in a significantly decreased AP firing rate relative to control neurons.
source: Inserting KCNT1 channels with SST kinetics into VIP and glutamatergic neurons indeed enhanced the GOF effects on input resistance and rheobase, and importantly, resulted in a significantly decreased AP firing rate relative to control neurons for both neuron types (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A2, B2, Supplementary file 3, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A2, B2, Supplementary file 3, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The relative sensitivity of SST and PV neurons, and resistance of VIP and glutamatergic neurons, to KCNT1 GOF is due to the differences in voltage dependence of the KNa current in each subtype.
source: This model-based evidence suggests that the relative sensitivity of SST and PV neurons, and resistance of VIP and glutamatergic neurons, to KCNT1 GOF is due to the differences in voltage dependence of the KNa current in each subtype.
evidence: This claim is inferred from computational modeling experiments manipulating activation curve parameters.

claim: INaP did not differ between WT and YH-HET SST neurons, either in the shape of the response or the peak amplitude.
source: In SST neurons, INaP did not differ between WT and YH-HET neurons, either in the shape of the response (Figure 7A, B), or the peak amplitude (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp experimental data measuring INaP shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: The peak amplitude of INaP was significantly increased by the Kcnt1Y777H variant in PV neurons.
source: In PV neurons, however, the peak amplitude of INaP was significantly increased by the Kcnt1Y777H variant (Figure 7C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp experimental data measuring INaP shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The mean peak amplitude of INaP in WT PV neurons was 70% larger than that in WT SST neurons.
source: Interestingly, the mean peak amplitude of INaP in WT PV neurons was 70% larger than that in WT SST neurons (−1.42 ± 0.16 to −0.85 ± 0.07 pA/pF; Figure 7B, D)
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp experimental data measuring INaP shown in Figure 7B and D.

claim: There may be differences in sodium channel expression, localization, or regulation inherent to SST and PV neuron types that confer their differential response to KCNT1 GOF.
source: Interestingly, the mean peak amplitude of INaP in WT PV neurons was 70% larger than that in WT SST neurons (−1.42 ± 0.16 to −0.85 ± 0.07 pA/pF; Figure 7B, D), suggesting there may be differences in sodium channel expression, localization, or regulation inherent to each neuron type that confer their differential response to KCNT1 GOF.
evidence: This claim is speculated based on observed differences in INaP between neuron types.

claim: An increase in INaP conductance, similar to what was seen in the experimental results (twofold), was sufficient to increase the number of APs fired in response to increasing current steps in model PV neurons.
source: Indeed, an increase in INaP conductance, similar to what was seen in the experimental results (twofold), was sufficient to increase the number of APs fired in response to increasing current steps (Figure 7E, F and Supplementary file 3), even in the face of the higher level of KCNT1 GOF (30 mM; Supplementary file 3 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 7E, F and Supplementary file 3.

claim: In model PV neurons with increased INaP, the rheobase current was decreased and the AP height was increased, like the experimental data.
source: Also, like the experimental data, the rheobase current was decreased (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 2) and the AP height was increased (80.4 ± 0.7 vs. 82.1 ± 0.8 mV).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The differential effects on AP firing in SST and PV neurons can be accounted for by the absence or presence of a secondary increase in INaP.
source: These results suggest that the differential effects on AP firing in SST and PV neurons can be accounted for by the absence or presence of a secondary increase in INaP.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental and modeling data showing the role of INaP.

claim: Homozygous expression of the Kcnt1Y777H variant increased connections between GABAergic neurons.
source: We previously showed that homozygous expression of the Kcnt1Y777H variant increased connections between GABAergic neurons (Shore et al., 2020), but heterozygous expression did not (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: There was an increase in homotypic synaptic connections of SST neurons in YH-HET networks (30/40 connections) relative to those in WT (15/40 connections).
source: Indeed, similar to the increase observed in I–I connections in YH-HOM networks, we found an increase in homotypic synaptic connections of SST neurons in YH-HET networks (30/40 connections) relative to those in WT (15/40 connections; Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by paired recording experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The amplitudes of the evoked postsynaptic currents (ePSCs) between connected SST neurons were not significantly different between the YH-HET and WT groups.
source: The amplitudes of the evoked postsynaptic currents (ePSCs) between connected SST neurons were not significantly different between the YH-HET and WT groups (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by paired recording experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Of the 20 WT SST neuron pairs tested, 12 were coupled, and the majority (9/12) of those were one-way chemical connections.
source: Of the 20 WT SST neuron pairs tested, 12 were coupled, and the majority (9/12) of those were one-way chemical connections (Figure 8C2).
evidence: This claim is supported by paired recording experimental data shown in Figure 8C2.

claim: Of the 20 YH-HET SST neuron pairs tested, 17 were coupled, and the majority (13/17) of those were two-way, or bidirectionally, connected.
source: Of the 20 YH-HET SST neuron pairs tested, 17 were coupled, and the majority (13/17) of those were two-way, or bidirectionally, connected (Figure 8C2).
evidence: This claim is supported by paired recording experimental data shown in Figure 8C2.

claim: Of the 3 bidirectionally connected WT SST neuron pairs, 2 were chemical and 1 was electrical.
source: Of the 3 bidirectionally connected WT SST neuron pairs, 2 were chemical and 1 was electrical, whereas of the 13 bidirectionally connected YH-HET SST neuron pairs, 7 were chemical and 6 were electrical (Figure 8C2).
evidence: This claim is supported by paired recording experimental data shown in Figure 8C2.

claim: Of the 13 bidirectionally connected YH-HET SST neuron pairs, 7 were chemical and 6 were electrical.
source: Of the 3 bidirectionally connected WT SST neuron pairs, 2 were chemical and 1 was electrical, whereas of the 13 bidirectionally connected YH-HET SST neuron pairs, 7 were chemical and 6 were electrical (Figure 8C2).
evidence: This claim is supported by paired recording experimental data shown in Figure 8C2.

claim: Heterozygous Kcnt1Y777H expression increases reciprocal connectivity among SST neurons, of both the chemical and electrical sort.
source: Thus, these data suggest that heterozygous Kcnt1Y777H expression increases reciprocal connectivity among SST neurons, of both the chemical and electrical sort.
evidence: This claim is inferred from paired recording experimental data on SST neuron connectivity.

claim: There was an increase in the sEPSC frequency onto NFS YH-HOM GABAergic neurons.
source: Finally, although we previously found no alterations in the sEPSC frequency onto the total population of YH-HOM GABAergic neurons, there was an increase in the sEPSC frequency onto those with an NFS phenotype (Shore et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: There was an increase in sEPSC frequency onto YH-HET SST neurons compared with that of WT.
source: Indeed, there was an increase in sEPSC frequency onto YH-HET SST neurons compared with that of WT (Figure 8D), suggesting a compensatory increase in excitatory drive onto the most impaired GABAergic subtype.
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The increase in sEPSC frequency onto YH-HET SST neurons suggests a compensatory increase in excitatory drive onto the most impaired GABAergic subtype.
source: Indeed, there was an increase in sEPSC frequency onto YH-HET SST neurons compared with that of WT (Figure 8D), suggesting a compensatory increase in excitatory drive onto the most impaired GABAergic subtype.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data on sEPSC frequency.

claim: YH-HET GFP-expressing neurons in slice fired fewer APs across all current steps than the WT GFP-expressing neurons.
source: Incremental current injections to elicit APs demonstrated a strong impairment in AP generation downstream of the heterozygous Kcnt1Y777H variant, as the YH-HET GFP-expressing neurons fired fewer APs across all current steps than the WT GFP-expressing neurons, similar to that observed in the YH-HET SST cultured neurons (Figure 9B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp experimental data in acute slices shown in Figure 9B and C.

claim: YH-HET GFP-expressing neurons in slice did not show a significant decrease in input resistance relative to those from WT.
source: Although YH-HET GFP-expressing neurons in slice did not show a significant decrease in input resistance relative to those from WT, they did show a large increase in rheobase current, without alterations in AP shape (Figure 9D).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp experimental data in acute slices shown in Figure 9D.

claim: YH-HET GFP-expressing neurons in slice showed a large increase in rheobase current, without alterations in AP shape.
source: Although YH-HET GFP-expressing neurons in slice did not show a significant decrease in input resistance relative to those from WT, they did show a large increase in rheobase current, without alterations in AP shape (Figure 9D).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp experimental data in acute slices shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The main electrophysiological finding from culture—the reduced excitability of YH-HET SST neurons—was confirmed in acute slices from YH-HET juvenile mice.
source: Thus, we confirmed the main electrophysiological finding from culture—the reduced excitability of YH-HET SST neurons—in acute slices from YH-HET juvenile mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of culture and slice experimental data.

claim: KCNT1-related epilepsy patients suffer with frequent, early-onset seizures, cognitive impairments, movement disorders, and sometimes additional behavioral and/or psychiatric problems.
source: KCNT1-related epilepsy patients suffer not only with frequent, early-onset seizures, but also with cognitive impairments, movement disorders, and sometimes additional behavioral and/or psychiatric problems (Bonardi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on KCNT1-related epilepsy patient phenotypes.

claim: KCNT1-related epilepsies remain highly refractory to current anti-seizure medications.
source: Unfortunately, after over 10 years of research efforts, KCNT1-related epilepsies remain highly refractory to current anti-seizure medications (Bonardi et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on treatment resistance.

claim: Recent work in heterologous cells has shown that KCNT1 GOF heteromeric channels, with WT and mutant subunits, exhibit KNa current increases that lie between those of WT and KCNT1 GOF homomeric channels.
source: Recent work in heterologous cells has shown that KCNT1 GOF heteromeric channels, with WT and mutant subunits, exhibit KNa current increases that lie between those of WT and KCNT1 GOF homomeric channels (Cole et al., 2021; Dilena et al., 2018; Rizzo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on heteromeric KCNT1 channels.

claim: Other recent studies have shown that heterozygous Kcnt1 GOF variant expression in neurons causes effects on KNa current and excitability that are intermediate to those of WT and homozygous variant-expressing neurons.
source: Furthermore, other recent studies have similarly shown that heterozygous Kcnt1 GOF variant expression in neurons causes effects on KNa current and excitability that are intermediate to those of WT and homozygous variant-expressing neurons (Gertler et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature on heterozygous KCNT1 GOF effects in neurons.

claim: Heterozygous and homozygous KCNT1 variant expression cause similar, gene-dose-dependent GOF effects at the current and neuron level, but not at the network or whole-animal level.
source: Furthermore, these data suggest that heterozygous and homozygous KCNT1 variant expression cause similar, gene-dose-dependent GOF effects at the current and neuron level, but not at the network or whole-animal level.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of heterozygous and homozygous experimental data across multiple levels.

claim: Several studies using LOF channelopathy models of both sodium and potassium channels have identified excitability effects on one neuron type without effects on another.
source: For instance, several studies using LOF channelopathy models of both sodium and potassium channels have identified excitability effects on one neuron type without effects on another (Hedrich et al., 2014; Soh et al., 2018; Tai et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on neuron-type-specific channelopathy effects.

claim: Other studies have shown that the same ion channel variant can cause opposite effects on excitability in different neuron types.
source: Other studies have shown that the same ion channel variant can even cause opposite effects on excitability in different neuron types (Makinson et al., 2016; Rush et al., 2006; Studtmann et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on opposite channelopathy effects in different neuron types.

claim: A recent study using a different KCNT1 GOF mouse model (human R474H, mouse R455H) showed KNa current increases selectively across positive potentials in glutamatergic, but across positive and negative potentials in FS and NFS GABAergic, neurons.
source: Moreover, these results are similar to those reported in a recent study using a different KCNT1 GOF mouse model (human R474H, mouse R455H), which showed KNa current increases selectively across positive potentials in glutamatergic, but across positive and negative potentials in FS and NFS GABAergic, neurons (Wu et al., 2024).

claim: A recent study showed that a potassium channel GOF variant causes opposite effects on excitability in the same neuron type from different brain regions (hippocampal CA1 vs. cortical layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons).
source: The idea of brain region-dependent effects of ion channel variants is not unprecedented, as a recent study showed that a potassium channel GOF variant causes opposite effects on excitability in the same neuron type from different brain regions (hippocampal CA1 vs. cortical layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons), and this opposite effect was suggested to be due to the compensatory upregulation of sodium channels in one neuron type but not the other (Varghese et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent literature on brain region-dependent channelopathy effects.
